title: US consumer sentiment slips to five-month low on inflation
article:
(Oct 23): US consumer sentiment edged down to a five-month low in October as high prices and rising interest rates depressed morale.

The University of Michigan’s final sentiment index eased to 48 from 48.1 in September, according to the survey released on Friday. Even so, that was an improvement from the preliminary reading and topped all estimates in a Bloomberg survey of economists.

Consumers expect prices to rise 4.7% over the next year, up from 4.6% in the previous month. They also saw costs climbing at an annual rate of 3.5% over the next five to 10 years. Both were the highest since May.

“After five years of above-target inflation, both short- and long-term inflation expectations have ticked up in recent months, exposing risks that elevated inflation expectations could become entrenched,” Joanne Hsu, director of the survey, said in a statement.

Consumer sentiment continued to deteriorate in October amid persistent inflation, tepid hiring and elevated mortgage rates. Prices at the pump remain well above US$4 a gallon, compounding longstanding frustrations with the cost of living.

See also: How to solve a US$40 tril debt problem? Donald Trump spilled the beans and nobody noticed

In recent months, price increases have outpaced pay gains, further pressuring household budgets. Data out last week showed consumer prices rose in September at the fastest pace in five months.

Economic issues like the cost of living remain front and centre for Americans in the final stretch of midterm campaigns.

See also: US mortgage rates decline for first time in nine weeks to 7.32%

“Consumers of all political persuasions agree that inflation is overwhelmingly the greater risk to the economy in the year ahead than unemployment,” Hsu said.

Sentiment among Democrats and Republicans improved somewhat in October, while sentiment among independents fell for a third straight month.

A gauge of buying conditions for durable goods fell to a record low in October, with the report citing higher interest rates and rising affordability concerns. Nearly 70% of consumers expect interest rates to rise in the year ahead, the highest in more than three years.

The current conditions gauge sank to the second lowest on record, while an index of consumer expectations improved for the first time since July.

The survey period includes responses from Sept 22 to Oct 19.

title: VietJet faces aircraft, cash seizures in FitzWalter debt fight
article:
(Oct 23): VietJet Aviation JSC faces seizure of ticket revenues and aircraft after a UK court appointed receivers to help recover more than US$250 million owed to a London-based buyout fund — effectively hobbling the carrier’s operations outside of Vietnam.

A London judge granted the order to a unit of FitzWalter Capital Ltd on Thursday, giving receivers from Alvarez & Marsal powers to take control of assets and redirect cash towards repayment of the debt.

The order goes significantly further than a worldwide freezing injunction imposed on VietJet just last week. Unlike that, it allows the receivers to intercept assets and cash flows that VietJet had previously been free to collect and use for its day-to-day operations.

That includes ticket-sale proceeds, with the receivers empowered to instruct travel agents, other airlines and credit-card acquirers to pay amounts due to VietJet directly to them, according to the receivership order.

They can also take delivery of new aircraft from manufacturers including Airbus SE and Boeing Co, seize and sell existing aircraft, engines and spare parts outside Vietnam. They can also collect money from VietJet’s overseas bank accounts as well as maintenance reserves and deposits held by lessors, and pre-delivery payments made to manufacturers.

See also: US agrees to buy at least 850 more F-35 fighter jets from Lockheed

The receivers can also seize VietJet’s interests in offshore subsidiaries, including entities in the British Virgin Islands, Singapore, Ireland and the Cayman Islands. Their powers include exercising voting rights, replacing directors, selling shares and procuring the winding up of companies.

Assets located in Vietnam are excluded from the order. VietJet is barred, however, from moving assets covered by the receivership into Vietnam, changing contracts relating to them without the receivers’ consent or otherwise taking steps that would undermine the receivers’ work.

VietJet and its directors are required to comply with the order, with breaches potentially amounting to contempt of court.

See also: American Airlines cuts outlook again, sees higher fuel bill this year

The company’s legal saga began in 2021, when it stopped making lease payments on four aircraft during the pandemic. The sum owed had grown to US$180 million by 2024 and has since topped US$250 million as the litigation dragged on. It’s unclear whether the company will appeal the latest ruling.

VietJet Group has 146 aircraft in its fleet as of Oct 23, according to industry data provider Cirium. The airline, which is the second largest in Vietnam, has major operations also in Thailand. The group also has in excess of 400 aircraft currently on order, the Cirium data also shows.

title: Amex to slash 5% of headcount as CEO seeks to reduce expenses
article:
(Oct 23): American Express Co is cutting 5% of its headcount globally as chief executive officer Steve Squeri seeks to keep a lid on the company’s rising costs.

Squeri told Bloomberg TV that the company has 78,000 employees, meaning the move will affect about 3,500 jobs.

Financial firms have been cutting jobs in recent months, with some companies attributing the changes to the increased use of artificial intelligence. This week, Barclays plc said it would eliminate 5,000 jobs. HSBC Holdings plc is planning job reductions across its UK wealth-management business, Bloomberg News reported earlier this month, and Citigroup Inc has also been lowering its headcount.

Squeri said on a call with analysts on Friday that the job cuts reflect the desire to make the company more agile and efficient, and find ways to reduce layers and speed up decision making.

The workforce cuts were announced after Amex posted third-quarter earnings that beat estimates, with adjusted earnings per share of US$4.68 surpassing the US$4.49 average analyst estimate in a Bloomberg survey.

The company also raised its full-year earnings guidance, saying it expects earnings per share of US$18.30 to US$18.60 in 2026, according to a statement on Friday. Previously, the figure was expected to be US$17.30 to US$17.90.

See also: US stocks drop as risk-off views dominate with oil up, Meta falling

But billed business — a measure of transactions on credit cards and other products — came in at US$454 billion in the third quarter (3Q), shy of the US$456.9 billion average estimate in a Bloomberg survey. The company said it had exited some small-business co-brand deals, which affected results.

That slower growth in billed business is likely a slight disappointment, according to Truist Securities analysts including Brian Foran.

“The headline is good — Amex beats on earnings and raises full year guidance,” the analysts said in a note to clients. “The details are more mixed.”

See also: Berkshire stock hits new high, moving on from Buffett’s exit

The company’s results were also affected by the sale of Amex’s equity interest in in Global Business Travel Group Inc (GBT), which resulted in a US$751 million after-tax gain. Amex used a portion of the gain to fund a US$253 million after-tax restructuring charge tied to efficiency initiatives. The gain, net of the restructuring, is excluded from the adjusted results.

“Our business momentum continues, with strength in billings, new acquisitions and card member retention, and excellent credit quality,” Squeri said in the statement.

The New York-based firm said expenses climbed about 9% to US$14.5 billion in 3Q, less than the US$14.8 billion estimate from analysts.

Amex has been refreshing certain cards, adding a raft of new perks last year to its Platinum card. Earlier this month, the company said it would work with Airbnb Inc to allow for certain luxury rentals on its travel site to count for the cardholders’ annual lodging credit. Chief financial officer Christophe Le Caillec had previously said to expect marketing expenses to increase by around 10% in the second half of 2026 compared with last year.

The company is also facing a US$350 million fine due to anti-money-laundering violations. The US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Reserve brought enforcement actions against Amex earlier this month, alleging deficiencies in the firm’s anti-money-laundering systems.

Amex said at the time that the penalty won’t affect the full-year 2026 guidance it previously issued or any 2027 outlook, and the orders don’t impose an asset cap on the firm.

title: AI tech fears push global credit spreads to 17-month high
article:
(Oct 23): Metrics across global bond markets are signalling their biggest risk-off sentiment in more than a year, as a selloff in artificial intelligence (AI) stocks and growing geopolitical tensions caused investors to seek out safe-haven assets.

On Friday, spreads on dollar bonds of higher-rated Asian companies widened to their highest levels since July 2025, moving in tandem with credit markets more broadly. That mirrors a jump in corporate bond yield premiums globally, which surged to their widest since May 2025, reaching up to 129 basis points (bps), a Bloomberg index shows.

“Credit risk is now calling the shots, and Asia cannot hide from the storm,” Natixis senior economist Gary Ng said. “There is a clear US risk aversion in AI-related investment and other global factors that may keep interest rates elevated.”

Mounting concerns over the rapid pace of debt-fuelled spending on AI is causing turmoil in markets amid fears that the technology won’t deliver profits soon enough. The sharp unwinding of AI bets has prompted debate among some prominent investors, with Citadel’s Ken Griffin warning of a bubble while Blackstone Inc president Jon Gray said there’s no cause for concern as demand is “almost parabolic”.

Euro investment-grade corporate bonds have followed suit, with index spreads hitting the highest since May 2025, the index shows.

See also: Paris unrest poses contamination risks to bond yields beyond France

Asian credit had pared some of its weakness, with spreads on regional credit-default swaps about one basis point wider, compared with 2bps earlier in the day, according to traders. Still, the surge in volatility prompted Export-Import Bank of Korea to postpone a yen bond sale.

Norbert Ling, Asia Pacific head of fixed income portfolio management at Invesco, said he remains constructive on credit as an asset class. “Wider spreads are giving investors more compensation for high quality credit risk,” he said.

The rout in the AI trade faded somewhat on Friday, offering investors some respite while Treasuries gave up some of the gains from the previous session’s rush for safety.

See also: US 10-year yield falls below 5% as investors flock to safe havens

Still, a gauge of the inverse relationship between US government bonds and AI-focused stocks has strengthened to levels last seen a year ago. It’s a sign the deepening tech selloff is sending investors back into bonds for safety.

“I see this as the beginning of a more sustained repricing of credit risk,” said Lakshmanan R, head of South and Southeast Asia corporates at CreditSights in Singapore. “It is the culmination of multiple global risks hitting markets one after another.”

Against that backdrop, Lakshmanan said he favours higher cash allocations and money-market instruments, as well as bank and financial-sector senior debt. Within credit, he prefers investment-grade over high-yield bets.

title: Axel Springer to cut Telegraph jobs after buying UK newspaper
article:
(Oct 23): Axel Springer SE is cutting roles at Telegraph Media Group Ltd (TMG), just months after the German company took control of the British newspaper publisher on the promise of fresh investment.

The newspaper will start a consultation period, with staff at risk receiving an email by midday, Telegraph editor Chris Evans and chief executive officer Carolin Hulshoff Pol said in an email to staff on Friday seen by Bloomberg News.

“These are difficult choices that we believe are necessary for the future of the business,” Hulshoff Pol wrote in the memo. It didn’t say how many cuts were being made.

The cuts signal a shift for the newspaper group under Axel Springer, which acquired TMG for £575 million in June, ending years of uncertainty over its future. The deal united two of Europe’s most influential conservative media brands under Axel Springer’s billionaire CEO Mathias Doepfner.

At the time, the German media group, which also owns Business Insider and Politico, pledged to back an investment programme “to grow and expand the business to enable it to become the leading centre-right media outlet in the English-speaking world.”

See also: UK set to ease up on senior bankers in bid to save firms £2 bil

Axel Springer subsequently parachuted in its own top managers to the UK group. Carolin Hulshoff Pol, formerly head of German title Bild, became CEO, while longtime executive Patrick Wehrmann was appointed as finance chief. Evans will remain in his position.

Under the changes, the publication plans to merge the comment and analysis teams, and combine features and lifestyle workers, Evans told staff at a meeting on Friday to announce the cuts.

“We will look to develop new revenue streams, and we will look to expand into overseas markets,” he said.

title: JSW Steel’s 2Q profit more than triples on higher prices
article:
(Oct 23): JSW Steel Ltd’s fiscal second-quarter (2Q) profit more than tripled beating expectations, as India’s infrastructure buildout drove prices higher.

Net income of the country’s biggest steelmaker by capacity increased 226% from a year earlier to 52.8 billion rupees in the three months through September, the company said in a statement on Friday. Analysts had forecast about 43.5 billion rupees, according to an average of estimates compiled by Bloomberg.

India’s steelmakers are preparing for prolonged growth in demand as the government invests heavily in public works. The nation’s steel consumption is expected to more than triple to 505 million tonnes by 2047, according to a draft policy released this month, setting the stage for a major expansion among producers. JSW plans to spend as much as 240 billion rupees in the next fiscal year to increase capacity.

The price of hot-rolled coil, part of JSW’s mainstay flat-steel operations, rose 21% over a year earlier to 59,902 rupees a tonnes in the three months through September, according to Kotak Institutional Equities. The company reported a 5% increase in production over the quarter to 7.27 million tonnes.

Revenue rose 21% on year to 544.9 billion rupees, while raw material costs increased 13% to 269.17 billion rupees.

title: Chery eyes producing cars in Canada as Chinese automakers circle the US
article:
(Oct 23): Chery Automobile Co is considering establishing local manufacturing in Canada, building on the launch of sales in that market next year and putting one of China’s biggest carmakers on the northern doorstep of the US.

While access to the US remains highly uncertain, Chery sees Canada as an important enough market to develop a deeper presence. Options being considered include taking over idle capacity at existing plants and working with partners, executive vice president Guibing Zhang said in an interview at Chery’s headquarters in Wuhu, China.

“Even without the American market, Canada is a market that is worth having a factory for manufacturing,” Zhang said. “We are looking for the suitable opportunity and communicating on the possible formats.”

If the plan is realised, Chery could be the first Chinese automaker to have a manufacturing presence in Canada, a major coup for Prime Minister Mark Carney’s efforts to bring investment into the domestic auto sector. But it also risks further straining ties with the US, given industry watchers view Canada as a launching pad for an inevitable entry by Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) into the American market.

Currently, hefty tariffs and technology restrictions effectively block Chinese EVs from American roads and officials have been clear that Chinese cars from Canada aren’t going to cross the border to the US. President Donald Trump has drawn a clear distinction between imports and production, suggesting in September that he may be willing to allow a Chinese automaker to build in the US and employ local workers.

See also: China's US$150 bil AI model stock slump shows no sign of easing

Chery executives have expressed ambitions to enter the US at some point. With the market closed off in the near-term, the carmaker is assessing idle capacity and speaking to investors in Canada who are interested in Chinese automakers, Zhang said, without identifying any companies.

Canada has rolled out the welcome mat to Chinese carmakers since striking a deal with Beijing to allow annual low-tariff imports of 49,000 of Chinese new-energy vehicles — a quota that will rise each year. Minister of Industry Melanie Joly visited China in June to meet with representatives from BYD Co, Geely Automobile Holdings Ltd and Chery, saying at the time that the companies were willing to explore joint ventures.

Zhang said that Chery’s vice president Charlie Zhang has been in frequent communication with Joly.

See also: How will China’s economy affect us?

Chery is gearing up to start sales in Canada next year, part of the high-stakes push by China’s automakers into overseas markets to make up for a slump in sales at home. While consumers are flocking to the cheaper, technology-focused models offered by the Chinese, the flood has sparked protectionist policies aimed at safeguarding domestic brands.

That, in turn, is pushing the Chinese to localise their production. Chery has a joint venture plant in Spain to help navigate European Union tariffs and quotas. It’s taken over a Nissan Motor Co factory in South Africa to establish a manufacturing hub for the continent, and is exploring making vehicles at Nissan’s Sunderland plant in the UK.

Rival BYD is also set to start selling cars in Canada. The world’s biggest EV maker has previously said it’s considering building a plant there, while it inquired about taking over an idled Stellantis NV plant in the Toronto suburbs to make buses, a local politician said in September. BYD previously operated a bus assembly plant in Ontario before it was shuttered in 2023.

Separately, Geely is set to start selling cars in Canada next year, though hasn’t said publicly whether it’s considering manufacturing there.

“If we can find some good ways to merge with partners, not only just from investments from Chery but from different parties, and if we can get the manufacturing going — I think that is something that the Canadian government would welcome,” Charlie Zhang said.

title: Unitree founder now expects robots breakthrough as soon as 2028
article:
(Oct 23): The founder of Unitree Robotics now expects a breakthrough in humanoids in as little as two years, a reversal for a Chinese entrepreneur who once predicted intelligent machines would take as long as decade to go mainstream.

Wang Xingxing, one of the country’s most celebrated tech leaders, has grown noticeably more bullish on his own industry since his company went public in the summer. The 36-year-old who created the nation’s biggest humanoid manufacturer a decade ago now predicts that, as soon as 2028, the machines can complete 80% of assigned tasks in the factory or home after receiving verbal orders — an arbitrary threshold he defines as the “aha” moment for practical robotic applications.

The comment marks an about-face in Wang’s belief on the timeline for humanoid robots — which have captured the popular imagination particularly in China, but remain largely a niche segment to serve researchers and enthusiasts. In August, Wang told the audience at the World Robot Conference in Beijing that it could take 10 years before they’re deployed on a massive scale at factories and homes to replace human labour.

Unitree Robotics G1 humanoid robots at the Embodied Intelligent Robot Industry Exhibition in Shanghai on Aug 12.

Now, the founder of the company known also as Yushu Technology Co says he’s had a change of heart because of incredible advances in artificial intelligence (AI) models like OpenAI’s GPT-6 in recent months. The model’s ability to guide humanoids through previously un-trained tasks — such as fetching goods — have generated buzz in the developer community on how AI is making progress in the physical world.

See also: ST Engineering’s new centre to test autonomous vehicles, drones and robots for cyber risks

“If you take a humanoid home now and ask it to clean the room, honestly I don’t think it can complete that task,” Wang told an industry conference in Hangzhou, according to a transcript of comments shared by his company. But that could become reality within a couple of years, he added. “I had some scepticism about AI model developers last year. But this year I see the most cutting-edge developers have begun letting their models improve themselves,” he said. “As long as you give a frontier model data and time, it will undoubtedly surpass humans in many areas.”

The extent of robots’ capabilities is a key question to investors who drove Unitree’s stock up five-fold on its debut in August. Venture capital firms and state funds have poured more than 100 billion yuan into backing startups in this field this year in China, according to investment tracker ITjuzi.

See also: QuikBot partners with Hitachi and Mitsubishi to prepare buildings for AI-powered robots

Still, some have grown more realistic about the usefulness of robots, particularly as competition intensifies and markets globally begin reassessing AI valuations. Unitree shares have waned since its debut month and are now down about a quarter from their August peak.

To prepare for the humanoid breakthrough, Wang said Unitree will expand production capacity to meet demand for potentially tens of millions of machines, compared to the tens of thousands it churns out every year. This massive demand would also buoy demand for AI chips, according to Wang.

Unitree is now using AI to look up research articles, write code and train humanoid models in simulation before testing in real environments. It then collects feedback to readjust the model. Wang said Unitree’s humanoids powered by the GPT-6 model can now draw pictures, changing colours and rinsing the palette along the way, as well as play Go, placing the pieces precisely on the tiny grid of a game-board.

“People have seen the progress of physical AI and model developers will pay more attention to machine intelligence and the robot industry,” Wang said. “We are developing our own models, while working with AI labs both at home and abroad, so that we can push physical AI to the tipping point faster.”

title: Accountancy grads of three local unis to enjoy module exemption for valuer qualification
article:
The Institute of Valuers and Appraisers Singapore (IVAS) has announced new collaborations to advance business valuation through new university pathways for aspiring valuation professionals, as part of a broader recognition of roles played by valuers in the changing business landscape.

Besides a refreshed Chartered Valuer and Appraiser (CVA) Programme curriculum, IVAS, which is under the umbrella of the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority, renewed its longstanding partnership with the International Valuation Standards Council (IVSC).

To broaden access to the CVA Programme, IVAS has granted module exemptions to three autonomous universities – Singapore Management University (SMU), Nanyang Technological University (NTU) and Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS).

These exemptions recognise the alignment of selected subjects in the universities’ Bachelor of Accountancy programmes with the relevant CVA Programme requirements.

Eligible graduates from the three universities will be exempted from one CVA Programme module, thereby reducing time and cost to attain the CVA qualification.

As the subjects that qualify graduates for the exemption form part of the universities’ Bachelor of Accountancy programmes, the initiative is expected to benefit more than 400 graduating students each year.

See also: The changing global financial landscape: Equities, debt and banking in transition

IVAS will continue working with universities to assess opportunities for further curriculum alignment and module exemptions, with the aim of creating more accessible pathways for graduates to attain the CVA qualification.

Also, to recognise that intangible assets such as intellectual property, brands and know-how now form the bulk of how many businesses are valued, the CVA Programme curriculum was refreshed for the January 2026 intake to include enhanced content on the valuation of intangible assets.

IVAS says the curriculum will undergo a further review in 2027 in preparation for new International Valuation Standards (IVS), which are expected to take effect in January 2028.

See also: Investing for your desired retirement lifestyle

Regular reviews of the CVA Programme will be made to ensure that it remains benchmarked against IVS and responsive to market developments.

According to IVAS, more than 150 professionals from Singapore and the region have enrolled in the refreshed CVA Programme since its launch in January 2026.

These new initiatives were announced at the IVAS-IVSC Business Valuation Conference 2026, held on Oct 23, drawing more than 800 participants from Singapore and the region, spanning the valuation, investment, and professional services communities.

Themed ‘Navigating New Realities in Corporate Markets”, this year’s conference marks the first time that IVAS and IVSC have collaborated with CFA Society Singapore, to create a platform for professionals from the business valuation and investment management communities to exchange insights and strengthen professional networks.

"Intangible assets today account for an ever-growing share of corporate value, and the decisions that businesses and investors make increasingly depend on rigorous, credible valuation," says Lie Kok Keong, IVAS Council Chairperson.

"The new university pathways, refreshed CVA Programme and renewed partnership with IVSC reflects IVAS’ commitment to ensuring the valuation profession keeps pace with these developments, remains globally connected and is accessible to the next generation of practitioners," he adds.

Cindy Tan Hwee Leng, President of CFA Society Singapore, says that as markets grow more complex and intangible assets take centre stage, the valuation and investment professions are becoming increasingly interconnected.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

"This collaboration between CFA Society Singapore, IVAS and IVSC creates a timely and valuable platform for practitioners from both communities to exchange insights, tackle emerging challenges together and build a deeper understanding of the evolving landscape," she adds.

Speaking at the conference, Indranee Rajah, Minister in the Prime Minister's Office says that while intangible assets often often drive a company's future growth, they are also more difficult to identify, measure, and compare.

"How well we understand these sources of value affects whether promising businesses can access financing, and whether investors can tell durable value apart from short-term expectations. Ultimately, credible valuation shapes capital flows towards productive and innovative businesses with strong fundamentals and long-term growth potential," says Indranee, who is also Second Minister for Finance and National Development.

She observes that in an increasingly difficult operating environment, marked by changes in supply chains and shifts in the cost of capital, valuation has become harder tasks.

"But it also makes reliable valuation even more important. Investors and businesses need assessments of value that are well-grounded in valuation and can withstand scrutiny. This is where valuers and investors can gain most from each other," says Indranee.

"Valuers bring rigour to the assessment of value. They examine the fundamentals and the assumptions that underpin it. Investors bring a market perspective. They consider those fundamentals alongside risk, opportunity and alternative uses of capital. Bringing these perspectives together can lead to more robust valuations and better investment decisions," she adds

title: AI data centre backlash threatens Australia’s US$70 bil dream
article:
(Oct 23): More than three-quarters of data centres set to be built around Australia’s biggest cities are at risk from stretched power grids and local opposition, threatening the country’s ambition to become an artificial intelligence (AI) hub for the Asia Pacific region.

Of the 40-plus large centres planned or under construction in Sydney and Melbourne — representing more than A$100 billion (US$70 billion or $90 billion) of projected investment — just 23% have confirmed publicly that they have secured electricity supply or grid connections, according to a Bloomberg review of company disclosure. Those agreements, a gauge of whether or not a project is advancing, suggest significant setbacks and potential delays.

Australia has bet heavily on a data-centre boom that is intended to capitalise on its vast open spaces as well as clean-energy potential. To date, though, most of the project pipeline is clustered around Sydney and Melbourne — where almost two in five of its inhabitants live — in order to harness existing fiber networks and reliable power. Those operations put more strain on already stretched infrastructure, and leave developers on a collision course with residents.

In Sydney, seven of 28 active projects have confirmed power, according to Bloomberg’s analysis. In Melbourne, the figure drops to three out of 15.

Bloomberg contacted 25 developers to verify public disclosure on power supply and the status of more than 40 projects. Operator GreenSquare declined to comment on its power arrangements but said it was “working closely with relevant authorities and infrastructure partners to support long-term operational performance”. CDC Data Centres said it had “robust delivery plans in place for all sites currently under construction” with power delivery timelines as anticipated.

See also: Apple is Wall Street’s favourite AI haven as spending fears hit

Nine others declined to comment or didn’t directly answer queries on future projects. The rest did not respond.

The consequences of friction and delays are already apparent. Operator Nextdc Ltd slashed its profit forecast this week after Melbourne residents blocked the installation of towering transmission lines, almost halving the value of its shares.

In Sydney, Goodman Group abandoned its A$1.2 billion Project Mars development last month. The proposed 90-megawatt facility would have been built about 20 metres from the nearest home and 160 metres from a public school, prompting hundreds of objections to be submitted during the planning process.

See also: SK data centre arm in talks to fund US$350 bil AI buildout in South Korea

“The social licence for Australian data centres is becoming an increasingly significant headwind,” Morgans Financial Ltd analyst Nick Harris wrote this week. “Investors are becoming concerned more delays could occur and question what the knock-on effect might be.”

The gulf between announced projects and those that will be built is also beginning to emerge in official data. Over a third of proposed data centres that would tap Australia’s main grid were cancelled last year, according to the Australian Energy Market Operator.

Part of the issue is the sheer scale of the build out. The country has more than 20 gigawatts of capacity in announced and early-stage data centre projects compared to an operational fleet of just 1.5 gigawatts, according to BloombergNEF.

“Access to energy is already a major issue,” said BNEF analyst Tushna Mehta. “Data centre capacity is being built much faster than the new generation needed to supply it.”

These hurdles are raising questions about the government’s push to make Australia a hub for the wider region, courting investors and seeking to streamline approvals even as practical constraints remain. Land may be plentiful, but data centres need access to high-voltage electricity lines and other infrastructure. Building further from the major cities can have advantages, but also means hefty investment in new transmission lines and telecommunications.

Sydney’s electricity grid is already struggling to accommodate the scale of the boom. Transgrid, which operates the statewide power network, said in August the city doesn’t have enough transmission capacity to connect any of the 20 gigawatts of inquiries it’s received from large new power users.

Half of that proposed demand has emerged within a 12km radius of its Sydney West substation, Transgrid said — equivalent to the peak winter electricity load of the entire state of New South Wales, in one small area.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

That strain is expected to intensify, and quickly. Australia already has more than 160 operating data centres, concentrated mainly in Sydney and Melbourne, which consume about 2% of electricity supplied by the country’s grids. AEMO has projected this could rise by a quarter each year to roughly 6% by 2030, and 13% by 2036.

AI is “the biggest new demand driver we have seen in electricity in 50 to 60 years”, said Ross Israel, the head of global infrastructure at Queensland Investment Corporation.

Another hurdle is access to water. Industry-commissioned analysis estimates Australian data centres use about 5.5 gigalitres of water each year, largely for cooling — equivalent to roughly 0.04% of national consumption. But the local impact could be far greater when projects are clustered together, including in growth corridors already facing stress from drought.

Residents living near Nextdc’s facility in Melbourne’s West Footscray — about 15 metres from it, in some cases — told a parliamentary inquiry last month they wanted compensation for noise, pollution and potential fire risks.

“What we are seeing is rising public resistance to AI, particularly generative AI,” said Bronwyn Cumbo, who researches data centres at the University of Technology Sydney. “Many are planned to be built near homes, schools, farmland and natural areas, and alter the experience and livability of these places.”

title: UK set to ease up on senior bankers in bid to save firms £2 bil
article:
(Oct 23): UK regulators plan to spare 139,000 bank executives from yearly checks under the senior managers and certification regime in an effort to spur growth and save firms almost £2 billion (US$2.7 billion or $3.4 billion) over a decade.

Staffers below senior manager level will no longer be subject to annual certification or appear on the financial services register, the Financial Conduct Authority and the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) said in proposals published on Thursday.

The reforms — the first big changes proposed under new PRA head Katharine Braddick — would also end the requirement for regulators to pre-approve chief actuaries and chairs of risk and audit committees, instead asking firms to notify regulators of these appointments.

Senior staff including chief executive officers, chief financial officers and chairs will still require regulatory pre-approval, including fit and proper tests. The wider conduct rules, which cover about 900,000 people, are not changing, though the regulators plan to simplify training and breach reporting.

“These proposals keep checks in place for the most important roles, meaning individuals are accountable for their actions, but reduce the administrative burden where it isn’t needed, giving firms more time to invest in growth-focused activities and greater flexibility in onboarding senior talent,” said Braddick, who was an executive at Barclays plc until earlier this year.

In total, companies will need to spend 53% less on complying with the regime, according to estimates in the consultation paper. The rules were introduced in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis to ensure executives at financial-services firms can be held to account for misconduct that occurs on their watch.

See also: Farage challenger faces £37,000 bill after losing court case

Lawmakers have been looking to narrow the scope of the rules for several years, with Conservative ministers announcing a review as part of the post-Brexit overhaul known as the Edinburgh reforms in 2022.

Regulators signalled last year that they would be streamlining the rules, as part of efforts by Keir Starmer’s Labour government to reduce regulation and spur much-needed economic growth. A consultation on the latest plans will now run until Jan 22.

“Firms will remain responsible for ensuring their employees remain competent, suitable and meet appropriate standards of conduct, and those no longer requiring pre-approval will continue to be held to the same level of accountability as before,” the regulators said in a joint statement.

See also: UK said to raise taxes on banks in budget this month

In a speech at London’s Mansion House late on Thursday, FCA CEO Nikhil Rathi said the regulator had “promised less intensive supervision for those clearly trying to do the right thing, so we can focus where harm is greatest. But the impact won’t be fully felt unless we also end tickbox compliance”.

Braddick used her speech at the event to announce the PRA will create a new directorate to focus on firms’ operational and cyber resilience. The strength of companies’ technology systems is under increasing scrutiny after a spate of cyber attacks spanning from crypto wallets to fridges.

title: Chinese market is gone for Western automakers, says Volvo CEO
article:
(Oct 23): Volvo Car AB plunged by about 30% to a record low after the Swedish automaker’s chief executive officer said the market for Western-developed cars in China is disappearing fast, prompting it to cut 2,500 more jobs.

Deliveries in China dropped more than 40% in the third quarter as local brands dominate the electric-vehicle market and a spending crisis weighs on demand. Volvo, owned by China’s Geely, is now valued at 29.8 billion kronor (US$2.68 billion or $3.83 billion), 80% less then when it listed five years ago.

“Nobody will be successful with the old recipe where you had global cars developed in Europe and sold them at a premium price” in China, chief executive officer Håkan Samuelsson said on Friday during an analyst call. “Those times are gone.”

The job cuts, affecting about 6% of Volvo Car’s workforce, are part of a plan to reduce costs by an additional five billion kronor. The latest round, targeting mostly Sweden, come on top of about 3,000 positions Volvo Car announced it would eliminate last year.

Volvo’s deeper savings measures mirror moves by manufacturers including Volkswagen AG and BMW AG, who are trying to become leaner to meet mounting Chinese competition. They are also stepping up local partnerships in China and development teams to come up with features to better target local tastes. Samuelsson’s comments suggest those steps may not go far enough.

BMW is set to start sales of its new iX3 sport utility vehicle in China next month, while the world’s biggest luxury-car maker in June slashed it outlook, citing dimming prospects in its biggest market. Volkswagen followed last month.

See also: Porsche locks-in on the super-sportscar segment with the Mission S

More than a hundred local brands are vying for buyers in China with the cut-throat competition forcing much fast model development times and lower prices. Western manufacturers like Volkswagen have been slow to react, and are lagging on some features favoured by domestic drivers, which have included gadgets like movie screens and advanced voice recognition.

Samuelsson admitted underestimating the rapid transformation of China’s car market. The Swedish brand, owned by China’s Zhejiang Geely Holding Co since 2010, will in future rely on technology and vehicle underpinnings from its Chinese parent to compete, Samuelsson said. Volvo, which listed in 2021, remains nearly 80% controlled by its parent, exacerbating share price swings.

“In China, you need to come back with regionally developed products with Chinese software, and there we of course have a huge advantage that we can work and develop those cars together with Geely,” he said during a Bloomberg Television interview.

See also: Performance Motors Limited introduces the PML One loyalty programme

Chinese brands are winning buyers with cheaper electric vehicles, advanced digital features and models tailored to local tastes. Western automakers, by contrast, have often relied on global models with higher prices and slower development cycles, leaving them struggling to keep pace.

Volvo’s troubles were evident when the company on Friday reported swinging to a loss that was much deeper than analysts had forecast. Aside from the issues in China, Volvo cited costs from tariffs in the US and the removal of electric-vehicle subsidies there.

To get back on track, the company plans to introduce seven new vehicles for Western markets and six regionally tailored models for China by the end of the decade.

In Europe, Volvo managed to grow sales even as competition there from Chinese brands is also intensifying. A European Union push to limit hybrid imports from the Asian country may provide only temporary respite as brands including BYD Co set up manufacturing in the region.

Samuelsson, who returned in April 2025 after leading Volvo for a decade through 2022, is preparing to hand over the CEO post to former Skoda boss Klaus Zellmer. The German manager is due to take over no later than Oct 1, 2027.

title: Turnover for 11 stocks with reduced board lot sizes traded 3.6% higher than broader STI stocks: SGX CEO
article:
The turnover for the 11 stocks selected for Singapore Exchange’s (SGX) 10-share board lot initiative is 3.6% higher than the broader stocks in the benchmark Straits Times Index (STI), says CEO Loh Boon Chye at the group’s 27th annual general meeting (AGM) on Oct 23.

The higher turnover reflects “broader participation”. SGX has also seen a greater proportion of individual participation, he adds.

On whether the bourse will consider further reducing the board lot size to one, Loh says it will be taken into consideration should there be a broader demand moving forward. He added that certain online and digital brokers’ platforms are already doing fragmented trading (double check if that’s the term).

SGX officially implemented the reduction of the standard board lot size for 11 counters on Oct 5. Securities priced $10 and above had their lot sizes reduced to 10 shares. The 11 counters are: DBS Group Holdings (DBS), Great Eastern Holdings, Haw Par Corporation, Jardine Cycle & Carriage (now Jardine Matheson Southeast Asia), Jardine Matheson Holdings, Keppel, Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation (OCBC), Prudential PLC, SGX, United Overseas Bank (UOB) and Venture Corporation.

On Oct 6, SGX said the reduced board lots saw an “immediate uptake”. The 10-share lots were “the most common trade size” in nine of the 10 actively traded stocks, led by DBS with around 5,000 trades.

When asked about adjusting fee structures, Loh noted that several brokers have already made adjustments or introduced significant fee cuts.

See also: Are Singapore SMID stocks losing their allure?

Chairman Koh Boon Hwee said the group will work with the ecosystem, but added that SGX is “not in the position” to mandate fees for the broker system.

On tokenisation and the fractional trading of shares and options, Loh said the group is evaluating to implement the tokenisation of securities collateral. The group is also studying the real economic outcome brought about by fractical options and securities. On fractional shares, he pointed out that this is being offered by “quite a number of brokers” today.

Other questions at the AGM focused on the group’s capital expenditure for FY2027. SGX announced, in its FY2026 results announcement, that expenses for the next financial year will increase by 6% to 8% and capex will come in at around $100 million. At the time, SGX said the monies will be invested in strategic priorities, platform modernisation and capability.

See also: Shadows of Black Octobers linger, but rays of support seen from healthy earnings

When asked about the overall return on investment, Koh said investors should look at the group’s overall return on equity (ROE), which will give an idea of what the group has had to invest to achieve that. The money, he added, isn’t spent on creating new products, but underlying IT infrastructure including our efforts to ensure our platform is as safe as possible.

In terms of buybacks, Koh says the group tries to buy back sufficient shares for its stock programme so it doesn’t dilute its shareholders.

On future prospects, Koh notes that the geopolitical environment is going to be a “little more fragmented than we are used to”.

“It’s something we’re going to learn to navigate,” he says.

title: Seatrium to undertake conversion and integration works on five whale class powerships
article:
Mainboard-listed Seatrium has secured a contract to undertake major conversion work and integration of five whale class powerships for Turkish power generation company Karpowership. Seatrium’s scope of work encompasses equipment integration, mechanical completion and pre-commissioning works.

Powerships are floating power plants equipped with hydrogen-ready multi-fuel generation systems and integrated onboard substations that connect directly to national electricity grids. Seatrium will work on the third-generation vessels that deploy up to 600 MW of immediate, grid-ready power.

Alvin Gan, executive vice president for repairs and upgrades at Seatrium, says: “This significant milestone marks Seatrium’s first major conversion work and integration of Karpowership’s whale class powerships. We are proud to support Karpowership’s drive to pioneer innovative floating power solutions and the next phase of its fleet development, bringing our capabilities in complex vessel integration and offshore engineering to the project.”

Karpowership chief technical officer Gokhan Kocak says, “We are pleased to build on our strong partnership with Seatrium, whose proven expertise in complex vessel integration make them an ideal partner.”

The contract marks the next step following an earlier letter of intent (LOI) signed in August 2025, solidifying the long-term partnership between the two companies. The LOI had provided for three floating, storage and regasification unit (FSRU) conversions and the potential integration of up to six new-generation powerships.

title: UK said to push for carve-out from new EU tech sovereignty rules
article:
(Oct 23): The UK has voiced concerns that the European Union’s (EU) push for technological autonomy will damage British digital companies, arguing that it should be eligible to compete for contracts under forthcoming “Made in Europe” tech rules.

The EU is debating whether to limit contracts under its Cloud and AI Development Act to European companies, its latest push for European preference rules as it seeks to reduce its dependence on non-European providers, like the US, according to people familiar with the matter.

The proposal is the centrepiece of a sweeping “tech sovereignty” package being drafted by Brussels, which will create a tiered system for cloud computing services and software providers — dictating that European governments rely exclusively on EU vendors to handle their most sensitive data.

The two sides are intensifying discussions on this and other matters ahead of an EU-UK summit in Brussels on Nov 20.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has raised the prospect of Britain rejoining the EU in the future, sparking expectations of a reset in EU-UK relations 10 years after the Brexit vote. In a speech last month to Labour Party members, Burnham said that Brexit had left the country weaker and failed to allow Britain to “take back control” of its borders and rules, as promised by the Leave campaign.

However, the EU’s push for European preference across a range of legislative files, from cars to public procurement, has irked the UK.

See also: AI video startup Higgsfield draws investment from Nvidia

The European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, did not immediately respond to comments. A UK government spokesperson said it’s closely engaging with the EU as the Cloud and AI Development Act develops, and will continue to make the case for close cooperation as a trusted partner. The spokesperson noted that the UK is already deeply integrated into Europe’s digital and technology ecosystem.

The new tensions over European preference rules center around two main objections from the UK side, according to people familiar with the discussions — the demand that digital services providers be physically based in the EU, and restrictions on ownership and control.

Britain is home to big telecommunications company and cloud providers, including BT and Nscale, which could be negatively impacted by the new rules.

See also: DeepSeek, MiniMax win approval for global use, state media says

Among the arguments made by the UK is that any move to exclude it breaches the terms of the post-Brexit trade deal that governs EU-UK relations, an argument refuted by the commission, according to people familiar with the matter.

The British government is under political pressure to align to Brussels on imposing tariffs on subsidised car imports from China in exchange for access to the EU-wide procurement model. France and Germany agreed a car deal last week which opens the door for the UK to qualify for European subsidies under “Made in Europe” rules set out by its forthcoming Industrial Accelerator Act. To benefit, however, the country will have to mirror EU’s rules on foreign direct investment and trade defence, a thinly veiled reference to measures the bloc has taken against China.

UK Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds signalled earlier this week he’s open to hitting Chinese electric vehicles with tariffs to win enhanced access to European markets, but would make the call based on UK needs not demands from the EU.

Among the other issues to be discussed at next month’s Brussels summit are greater alignment on rules governing transport of agriculture and food products, linking their cap-and-trade emissions programmes and greater access for young people to live and work in both jurisdictions, one of the most contentious aspects of the talks.

title: Eni raises investor payouts as high fuel prices boost cash flow
article:
(Oct 23): Eni SpA said it will return more cash to shareholders after the Middle East war drove up energy prices and sent refining margins soaring.

The Italian oil and gas producer will pay an extraordinary dividend of about €1.3 billion (US$1.5 billion) and increase its 2026 share buyback to €3.8 billion from €3.4 billion, according to a statement on Friday. It previously raised the buyback in April and again in July.

Europe’s oil companies have benefitted from exceptionally strong refining margins this year, with gains in prices for products such as diesel far outpacing those in crude. Milan-based Eni has also expanded its global oil and gas production portfolio and project ramp-ups are further buoying the bottom line.

Adjusted net income was €2.8 billion in the third quarter, beating the €2.5 billion average analyst estimate. Net cash from operations was €4.36 billion, compared with an estimate of €4.33 billion.

title: AI video startup Higgsfield draws investment from Nvidia
article:
(Oct 23): Higgsfield Inc, an AI video startup founded by a former Snap Inc executive, said it has attracted investment from Nvidia Corp and TCV to help fund global infrastructure and hiring to capture growing demand.

The San Francisco-based company has the majority of its engineering talent in Kazakhstan, and its announcement is part of Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s visit to the country. Billing itself as a specialist service for brands and creators looking to generate media and content at scale, Higgsfield said its registered users have grown to more than 40 million. The new funding is part of an extension to its Series B round in August, which raised US$400 million at a US$5.4 billion valuation led by DST Global. Higgsfield didn’t disclose the latest valuation or the size of the extension.

Video generation with artificial intelligence tools is notoriously capital-intensive, but startups in this sector have shown user engagement and drawn investor interest. China’s Kling AI, owned by Kuaishou Technology, this summer raised US$2.8 billion at about a US$15 billion valuation. Higgsfield’s US rival Runway AI Inc raised US$315 million at a US$5.3 billion valuation in February, which also had Nvidia participating.

Paying customers are increasingly joining AI video services like Higgsfield, which said it had added 10 million since its summer fundraising. TCV, a growth-stage fund that’s previously backed Netflix Inc, Spotify AB and ByteDance Ltd, said it’s investing in the AI video startup because it’s shown “a radically faster, professional-grade and AI-native mechanism for creators, brand marketers and agencies alike to turn ideas into images and video”.

Founded in 2023 by former Snap executive Alex Mashrabov and Kazakhstani AI engineer Yerzat Dulat, Higgsfield’s AI video-generation platform is on track to surpass US$1 billion in annualised revenue based on its current performance, Mashrabov said last month.

Higgsfield serves as a platform to access about 35 AI video models from other providers along with its own AI engine, allowing creators to access and combine those competing technologies. Users can select different models for various parts of a production, from storyboarding and character creation to audio and finished video.

See also: DeepSeek, MiniMax win approval for global use, state media says

title: China's US$150 bil AI model stock slump shows no sign of easing
article:
(Oct 23): There’s no end in sight for the sell-off in China’s artificial intelligence (AI) model developer stocks, with competition growing ever more heated and the threat of rival listings next year.

MiniMax Group Inc and Z.AI Co, also known as Zhipu, have shed a combined US$150 billion ($192 billion) in market value from their respective highs as of Thursday's close. The slide marks a brutal reversal after the duo’s hotly anticipated market debuts in January.

Domestic AI firms continue to slash token prices, while global giants Anthropic PBC and OpenAI have followed suit in order to minimise Chinese models’ cost advantage. Meanwhile, potential initial public offerings (IPOs) by DeepSeek and Moonshot AI could divert investor cash away from MiniMax and Zhipu, the only listed Chinese pure plays.

“Zhipu and MiniMax need to figure out how to win in the long term,” said Leonid Mironov, a portfolio manager at Gavekal Capital. “Between US models being better, and DeepSeek being most efficient, it’s hard to pinpoint exactly where MiniMax and Zhipu could go.”

The new M3.1 Flash model released by MiniMax on Monday provided no lift for its stock, despite sharply reduced token costs and improved performance. Zhipu has seen a similarly cold reaction to the launch of its GLM-5.3-FlashX in September.

See also: In China, rank comes first

According to the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, the pair’s latest offerings are far behind models from the US leaders in terms of intelligence. They even slightly trail DeepSeek, Alibaba Group Holding Ltd and Xiaomi Corp amid the continued flood of new products vying for usership.

“China currently has more than 10 AI labs, but eventually will be consolidating to less than that,” said Alex Liu, an analyst at Bank of America Corp. “Right now it’s actually hard to say who’s going to survive or who’s going to be the first to drop off.”

On the plus side, Chinese models continue to dominate global usership. DeepSeek and MiniMax have now won approval to deploy models overseas, state media reported on Thursday. MiniMax shares rose as much as 5.8% on Friday, while Zhipu’s gained 4.8%.

See also: China said to tighten scrutiny of listed company spinoffs — Bloomberg

MiniMax already gets most of its revenue from outside of China, while Zhipu’s application programming interface (API) is gaining traction with global developers, JPMorgan Chase & Co strategists including Chloe Liu wrote in a note this week. The bank is bullish on Z.AI over MiniMax, seeing the former better positioned due to its coding capability.

The pair are still unprofitable, however, and global price wars make the bottom line outlook even tougher.

“Labs that lead on capability and paid API growth break even earlier than peers,” JPMorgan’s Liu wrote. AI models and applications should turn profitable “around 2028”, though the market remains focused on revenue mix for now, she added.

In addition to worries over competition, profitability and new Chinese AI stock offerings, Zhipu and MiniMax may also see pressure from looming share lock-up expiries. About 178 million Z.AI shares and 25 million MiniMax shares held by pre-IPO investors are due to become eligible for trading in January, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

title: US proposes curbs on investment in Chinese biotech firms
article:
(Oct 23): The Trump administration is seeking to restrict American investment in Chinese biotechnology companies, potentially complicating financial ties at a time when US drugmakers are increasingly turning to China for new medicines.

The Treasury Department on Thursday proposed adding biotechnology to a list of sensitive technologies subject to investment limits involving foreign adversaries, citing national security concerns.

The proposed regulations would require American investors to notify the government about certain transactions involving foreign companies developing sensitive technologies and prohibit others entirely. The rules would expand an existing program targeting investments in areas including artificial intelligence (AI), semiconductors and quantum computing.

The move represents the latest escalation in Washington’s efforts to rein in China’s biotech advances. Last year, Congress passed the Biosecure Act to restrict federal agencies and government-funded companies from using or procuring services from designated Chinese biotech firms, although the restrictions were weaker and narrower than initially proposed.

Shares of Chinese biotech companies fell, with Genscript Biotech Corp dropping as much as 14% in Hong Kong. Insilico Medicine Cayman TopCo slid 5.2%, Duality Biotherapeutics Inc fell 3.9%, CSPC Pharmaceutical Group Ltd lost 3.4%, Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals Co declined 3% and Innovent Biologics Inc slipped 2.2%.

The US tightening comes as Beijing is also adjusting its own approach. In a sign of biotechnology’s growing strategic importance, China last week proposed adding several biomedical technologies to its export-control list — though its plan explicitly allows licensing deals for drugs to continue.

See also: US, China release product lists for US$30 bil tariff deal

Chinese biotechnology companies have become a source of innovation for the pharmaceutical industry. US drugmakers are increasingly turning to China to license promising treatments as they search for new products to replenish their pipelines.

Licensing deals aren’t expressly prohibited under Washington’s proposed rules, according to Duane Wright, a senior healthcare policy analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence. The restrictions won’t take effect until that process is complete.

Wright said the Treasury proposal begins with a “very broad definition” of biotechnology — covering small molecules, biologics, vaccines and cell and gene therapies — but leaves room to narrow the pharmaceutical provisions after stakeholder comments. Transactions such as equity investments and joint ventures are most clearly affected, he added.

See also: Xi seizes Trump detente to seek lasting gains on trade, Taiwan

“This is still the opening stage of the rule-making, so the scope could change before the rule is finalised,” Wright said.

The proposed regulations would also restrict investment in Chinese brain-computer interface companies, a growing field of start-ups that aim to build technologies that allow people to control electronics directly with their brains. China and the US both have burgeoning brain tech industries, with start-ups racing to develop implants, helmets and other devices.

Industry groups including the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America, the Biotechnology Innovation Organization and Incubate, a coalition of life sciences venture capital investors, warned that an overly broad approach could create unintended consequences for American biotech companies and public health.

“The details of the proposed Treasury Department rules matter,” John Crowley, the president of BIO, said in a statement. “We cannot restrict our way to success.”

title: SGX should begin planning ahead for ‘eventual transition’ in CEO role: SGX’s Loh Boon Chye
article:
Singapore Exchange (SGX) should begin planning ahead for the “eventual transition” for the role of CEO, announced CEO Loh Boon Chye at the group’s annual general meeting (AGM) on Oct 23.

“We are doing so from a position of strength – with a clear strategy, strong momentum and a highly capable leadership team. This gives us the opportunity to plan thoughtfully and with confidence for the future,” he says.

Loh, who was appointed SGX’s CEO on July 14, 2015, notes that his current contract runs until the middle of July 2027, which leaves the group with “ample time” to “plan thoughtfully” and work through the arrangements together. The group has not set a specific date for the transition.

What matters, Loh adds, is that the group gets the transition right, done in the “best interests of the company, our people and our shareholders - and keeping SGX’s momentum and ambitions firmly on track”.

“My ambitions for SGX are greater than ever. We have built the foundations to aim higher, move faster, and achieve much more. I want us to accelerate our growth, expand our global reach and take SGX to a new level. That is what I intend to drive forward,” he says.

“We have built something strong together. And I genuinely believe our best opportunities are still ahead of us,” he adds.

See also: XMH Holdings to appeal $10.2 mil tax bill for FY2024; slapped with $12.5 mil tax for FY2025

He lauded Loh’s achievements, noting that SGX was in the middle of a “crisis” when the CEO first joined.

“I remember reading about the outages. He worked really hard over the next two to three years to stabilise the situation, to ensure that our IT systems were up to snuff,” he said. “The fact that SGX had a relatively smooth ride on the IT front is a tribute to the amount of work he put in today.”

See also: Christie’s International Real Estate launches in the Maldives

Koh also highlighted Loh’s work in developing the strategy to transform SGX from a cash equities market to a global multi-asset platform.

“Derivatives, as we have discussed, is a really big part of the business,” he said.

“While things like ETFs and Singapore depositary receipts (SDRs) and other things are small today, don’t forget [that] all of these businesses start that way. Choosing not to do it is choosing not to participate,” he added. “While it has grown, we continue under Boon Chye’s leadership and look at emerging areas. He has articulated his confidence for some of these things in future.”

Koh also noted that Loh “isn’t going to go away anytime soon”. “Being the manager he is, he has definitely set into motion a transition that is going to be made as professionally as he can. And he has, especially in the last couple of years, set the foundations for the future in our cash equities market by his active participation first in the Equity Market Review Group and now in the EQDP.”

“We can continue to build on that, I believe that the company has done really, really well under Boon Chye’s leadership,” he added.

Since Loh’s arrival in July 2015, SGX’s shares, till June 30, are up 216%. Its NPAT is up 112% while the market cap for the group rose 252%.

title: DeepSeek, MiniMax win approval for global use, state media says
article:
(Oct 23): DeepSeek and MiniMax Group Inc have won approval to deploy models overseas, part of a wave of homegrown AI technologies that Beijing will allow to operate globally, a Chinese state media affiliate said.

Much of Chinese AI will remain free for export, according to a post published by Yuyuantantian, a social account affiliated with state broadcaster China Central Television. It addressed Beijing’s draft proposal last week for export control measures that would restrict certain artificial intelligence tools and services, including large language models and agents.

The proposed restrictions could limit overseas access to China’s most advanced models, potentially slowing an international surge in adoption driven by cost-effective Chinese open-source AI.

“Since the policy was announced, leading companies DeepSeek and MiniMax have successfully completed the registration process, as well as the procedures for open-sourcing and authorising overseas use,” according to the post published late Thursday by Yuyuantantian. “AI companies can continue their commercialisation efforts as usual.”

Chinese startups have made significant strides closing the gap on US market leaders this year. Beyond more affordable pricing, they’ve also attracted users by making their models easier to customise than proprietary systems like the ones on offer from OpenAI and Anthropic PBC. Beijing’s interest in controlling the export of what’s seen as strategically important technology has shown up most prominently in the way it forced the unwinding of Meta Platforms Inc’s acquisition of Manus, an AI agent startup with Chinese roots.

China regularly updates its catalog of technologies that are prohibited or restricted from export. In 2020, Beijing added algorithms to the list, after the first administration of US President Donald Trump threatened to ban TikTok unless the app sold its US assets to an American company.

See also: OpenAI shifts value to US$1.25 tril as funding talks finalise — Bloomberg

The latest revisions have been in development since the first half of the year, with government departments consulting and integrating feedback from research institutions and industry participants, Yuyuantantian said. The post stressed that the catalog aims to “define boundaries rather than simply restrict the export of AI technology.”

There are significant carveouts to the proposed regulations. Providing API access, web applications or software-as-a-service features will not be subject to export restrictions, even if powered by restricted underlying models, according to the post.

The post contrasted Beijing’s approach with that of Washington, accusing the US of using targeted export bans and technology blockades to protect its competitive dominance.

See also: Tesla’s lowered capex target fuels doubt on AI, robotics goals

“China, however, is not following this path,” the post added.

title: Apple is Wall Street’s favourite AI haven as spending fears hit
article:
(Oct 23): It’s become one of the most reliable trades in the stock market as sentiment towards artificial intelligence (AI) swings wildly: Whatever AI stocks do, Apple Inc does the opposite.

The iPhone maker’s stock is up 27% in 2026, making it the biggest contributor to the S&P 500 Index’s 12% climb. It’s also by far the best performer among the Magnificent Seven technology giants this year, a stark reversal from 2025, when its 8% gain put it near the bottom of the group.

The reason for the divergence is fairly simple. While most mega-cap tech companies are spending wildly on AI infrastructure, Apple is largely sitting it out and instead focusing on what it historically does best, creating products that get consumers buzzing, like its new foldable iPhone Duo. With Wall Street’s view towards AI capital expenditures seemingly in constant flux, the company’s shares have become investors’ preferred method for staying in Big Tech while avoiding some of the group’s ups and downs.

“Apple is a very liquid hedge against AI volatility, and it’s a great position to have if you are starting to get worried about AI but still want tech exposure,” said Jordan McCall, a senior portfolio manager at Russell Investments, which has US$434 billion ($555 billion) in assets and owns the company’s shares in multiple portfolios. “Apple is a flight to safety when the market gets nervous.”

The divergence was clear on Thursday, when Apple rose as much as 1% and was the only Magnificent Seven stock in the green, while the broader market fell with chip stocks leading the way down, after results from Lam Research Corp and Meta Platforms Inc raised questions about AI spending.

Investors are searching for safety because sentiment around AI is shifting so quickly. Shares of the big spenders like Microsoft Corp, Amazon.com Inc, Alphabet Inc and Meta Platforms Inc, and the chipmakers at the heart of AI infrastructure, rise and fall as Wall Street debates when and if the hundreds of billions in capital expenditures will pay off in a big way. Apple has an increasingly negative correlation to semiconductor stocks and often moves in the opposite direction of its mega-cap peers.

The dynamic was apparent last week, when concerns about cloud computing provider CoreWeave Inc’s debt spurred widespread selling of AI stocks. The SOX tumbled more than 11%, marking its worst week since April 2025, while an index of Magnificent Seven stocks sank 3.1%. Apple, meanwhile, rose 2% as the company said demand for the Duo was “nothing short of extraordinary”.

“If hyperscalers get more bad news, it would make sense to sell the SOX and use the money as a source of funds to buy Apple,” said Michael Matousek, the head trader of US Global Investors Inc. “Apple is more of a defensive play because it lacks exposure to the themes moving chips, and given how pronounced this kind of pair trade has become, it is so much easier to just go with the momentum. I wouldn’t fight it.”

See also: SK data centre arm in talks to fund US$350 bil AI buildout in South Korea

Apple’s 40-day correlation to the chip index has been negative since early July and is at its most extreme in data going back to 1994. On a 10-day basis, Apple has a negative 90% correlation with the chip index, according to Jonathan Krinsky, the chief market technician of BTIG.

Apple’s strong free cash flow and durable earnings growth are helping it stand out, McCall said. Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta have seen their free cash flow plummet or even turn negative as they invest in AI infrastructure. And while chipmakers are seeing huge growth for the time being, the fear is their earnings will nosedive if that spending slows.

The primary concerns for Apple shareholders are that it’s growing more slowly than its Big Tech peers but carries a soaring stock market valuation. The company is scheduled to report earnings for its fiscal fourth quarter in a few weeks, and revenue is expected to rise about 15% for the year, well below the overall tech sector, according to Bloomberg Intelligence data. What’s more, the pace is expected to slow to 9.7% in fiscal 2027 and to 5.5% in fiscal 2028.

Meanwhile, the shares trade at 36 times earnings estimated over the past 12 months, their highest multiple since January 2008. That’s twice Nvidia Corp’s valuation and well above where the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index and S&P 500 trade.

This combination could make it difficult for Apple to continue outperforming, especially if investors’ perceptions of big AI spenders and chipmakers improves again.

“With SOX having just seen a 16% pullback, and Apple at all-time highs, we think a bounce in SOX is likely to coincide with Apple pulling back, at a minimum, towards its 50 DMA,” BTIG’s Krinsky wrote on Oct 19, referring to Apple’s 50-day moving average, which was 4.7% below the stock’s most recent closing price.
